article.title: What the World Needs Now
article.author: Desi Cortez
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Today, the sun is cold, and this new day, well, honestly, it already seems old... It seems, to these eyes, 'What the world needs now is love, sweet love.” Once upon a time, on what was unquestionably a much more hopeful American afternoon, those words floated through battery-powered radios, living rooms you couldn't sit in…, supermarkets where Sugar Babbies, Powerhouse bars, and Black Cows cost 15 cents, school assemblies, and Coca-Cola commercials sounded like little musical promises. They suggested humanity might eventually grow tired of bloodshed, hatred, greed, racial hierarchy, religious warfare, and the exhausting full-time job of despising strangers. Perhaps, just maybe, after enough suffering, we would finally acquire some uncommon common sense, sit down together, share the bread, pass the bottle, pass the dobie, and stop treating human difference like probable cause. Related: Choosing Each Other: The Most Defiant Act in American Politics Those words were never more apt than right here and right now—precisely because the world seems determined to do the exact, total, complete opposite. We are living through a bare-knuckled battle between equality and superiority, democracy and domination, community and tribal conquest: Compare and contrast - One side argues that every human being possesses equal worth, equal dignity, and an equal claim upon the future. The other side still believes the world is a private country club, membership inherited at birth, with the 12 Disciples supposedly bouncing the velvet rope. One side wants to widen the table. The other is counting the silverware, checking identification, and asking who invited all these different people. And now push has come to shove. That phrase is often used casually, as though describing a disagreement over parking spaces or the last rib-eye at the bi-annual family reunion. But this push is historical. It is the long, relentless push of people who were told to wait, kneel, obey, assimilate, accommodate, blend in, alas, disappear, or be extremely grateful for whatever crumbs fell from the banquet table. Women pushed. Black people pushed. Workers pushed. Immigrants pushed. Indigenous people pushed. Gay and transgender people pushed. Disabled people pushed. Every group denied the full inheritance of humanity eventually placed both hands against the locked door and leaned forward. The shove is we, the unwashed and unwanted, the little people’s backlash. It is the frightened fury of those who confuse equality with individual personal loss. They hear “share the country” and somehow translate it as “surrender the plantation.” They experience another person’s freedom as an “eviction” notice. A Black mayor, a lady president, a Muslim congresswoman, a gay teacher, a Latino judge, an Asian business owner, a transgender neighbor—none of these people must do anything threatening. Their mere presence in positions once reserved only, I scream ONLY for a particular class, color, gender, and pedigree is treated as an invasion. That is the sickness beneath much of our present political pandemic, MAGA16: too many people do not merely want a place in society; they demand their old unearned and undeserved place atop society. Consequently, “love” can no longer mean smiling politely while somebody measures your humanity with a crooked ruler. Harmony cannot mean the oppressed singing softly enough not to disturb the comfortable. Peace is not the absence of noise while cruelty quietly conducts business behind gold-plated closed doors. There is no moral virtue in remaining calm while somebody methodically removes your rights, deports your neighbors, rewrites your history, raids your schools, strips your voting power, and then scolds you for raising your voice. Love without courage is merely good manners wearing Grey Flannel or Aramis, two of my favorite vintage colognes. Real love is not weak in the knees, meek, all soft and sugary, or spineless. It does not sit cross-legged in a meadow, star-gazing while fascist Trumpism drives a bulldozer through the neighborhood. Love protects. Love confronts. Love tells the stone-cold truth when little white lies have become more profitable. Love stands between the bully and the bruised. Love feeds the hungry, shelters the homeless, heals the sick, educates the child, enlightens those who are in the dark, welcomes the stranger, and refuses to ask whether human suffering, at the dirty, bloody hands of oppression and exploitation, has completed the proper paperwork. Sweet love sometimes has to show its teeth. Perhaps there’s that time n’place where push has come to shove, and you may have to show your ass, act a fool up in there, I’m just sayin’. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke of love, but he did not mean spineless surrender. Fannie Lou Hamer preached justice, but she was not asking Mississippi politely to reconsider the American version of apartheid, whenever convenient. Congressman Adam Clayton Powell spoke of ‘Audacious Power.” Frederick Douglass understood that power concedes nothing without a demand. Harriet Tubman’s love wore boots, carried a pistol, traveled at night, and did not pause for a bipartisan committee hearing. Their love was not passive. It was organized, disciplined, stubborn, and dangerous to the injustices that surround them. That is the kind of love this moment requires—not classic Hallmark greeting-card love, commercial-jingle love, or the decorative “thoughts and prayers” love offered after every perhaps preventable tragedy. We need, excuse me, “prison-buff” muscular love, think Devil's Isle or Alcatraz: love with a spine much stronger than our current “Gumby” edition. We require love with a memory, a 3-Tier Star Trek strategy, and a voter-registration card. Love capable of marching, organizing, boycotting, striking, teaching, protecting, and refusing to cooperate with, note this: organized cruelty. Organized inhumanity. Organized Heartlessness As the Spinners put it, we need a Mighty. Mighty Love Yes, I would like to teach the world to sing in perfect Easter Sunday Baptist Church harmony. But harmony does not require everyone to sing the same note. That is not harmony; that is, check this now - authoritarian karaoke. Harmony is created when different, i.e., diverse voices are allowed to exist fully—soprano and bass, sacred and secular, immigrant and native-born, Black and white, gay and straight—without one section snatching the microphone, unplugging everybody else, and declaring itself the national anthem. What section could that be? Yes, this world does need love, sweet love. But that love must be more than a pleasant elevator soundtrack playing while democracy is mugged, raped, forcibly sodomized, if not suffocated, murdered in a dark-ass alley. Push has come to shove because superiority will not peacefully surrender the throne it delusionally believes baby Jesus, History 101, skin tone, wealth, or weaponry assigned to it. Equality, meanwhile, can no longer survive on patience, symbolism, and polite appeals to consciences that packed up and left town years ago. So yeah, let us sing! Sing loudly. Sing defiantly. Sing together. Sing every forbidden verse until the walls of injustice tremble and the guardians of oppression lose their appetite for silence. But while we're singing, we'd better be organizing, mobilizing, and raising a little righteous hell. Because the world desperately needs love. But in times like these, love needs more than a beautiful melody. Love needs courage, conviction, a backbone, and an army of good people willing to stand up and fight for it. After all, you can't sing a bully into having a conscience.
